name: Somatoform Disorder
pinyin: qū tǐ xíng shì zhàng ài
preview_text: The location, quality, and triggers of your physical symptoms aren't random - they point to which organ system is out of balance. Most people with somatoform disorder see meaningfu...
conventional_description: Somatoform disorder (now more commonly called somatic symptom disorder) involves persistent physical complaints that cause significant distress and disrupt daily life, yet no underlying medical condition can fully explain them. Common symptoms include chronic pain, gastrointestinal problems, fatigue, and neurological-like sensations such as numbness or dizziness. Diagnosis is clinical, based on the pattern and impact of symptoms rather than a single test, and it often coexists with anxiety or depression.
conventional_treatments: Standard care typically includes cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to help reframe the relationship with symptoms, and antidepressant medications (SSRIs or SNRIs) that can reduce both emotional distress and physical discomfort. Pain management strategies and regular supportive medical visits are also common. The aim is to improve functioning and reduce the intensity of symptom focus.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views somatoform disorder primarily as a disruption in the body's flow of Qi, the vital substance that animates every function. When Qi moves smoothly, the body feels light and comfortable. When it stagnates - often because of unresolved emotional stress - physical symptoms emerge. The Liver organ system is the first to be affected, as it governs the free flow of Qi. Constrained Liver Qi creates pressure, distension, and wandering aches, and it can directly impact the digestive system and the mind.
If the stagnation persists, it begins to affect other organ systems. The Spleen, which transforms food into energy, becomes weakened - leading to fatigue, bloating, and loose stools. Over time, this weakness generates dampness and phlegm, a heavy, sticky substance that clogs the channels and produces sensations of heaviness, numbness, and brain fog. This explains why many people with somatoform disorder feel as if they are moving through mud.
Emotional strain can also generate heat, which rises to harass the Heart and its housing of the mind. This results in palpitations, insomnia, and a restless, agitated feeling. Meanwhile, long-term stress and overwork can deplete the Kidney's deep reserves of Yin, the cooling and moistening foundation of the body. Without enough Yin, chronic soreness, night sweats, and a sense of inner heat take hold. Each of these patterns produces a different set of symptoms, which is why two people with the same diagnosis can feel completely different - and need different treatments.
classical_quote: 「妇人咽中如有炙脔，半夏厚朴汤主之。」
classical_translation: "When a woman feels as though there is a piece of roasted meat stuck in her throat, Ban Xia Hou Pu Tang governs it. This describes the classic 'plum-pit Qi' sensation, a key feature of somatoform disorder arising from Liver Qi Stagnation and Phlegm obstruction."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what your physical discomfort feels like and when it strikes. Since somatoform disorder almost always starts with unresolved emotional strain, the first clues are how symptoms relate to stress, frustration, or low mood. The quality, location, and timing of the discomfort guide the diagnosis toward one pattern or another.
If the discomfort moves around - chest tightness, rib-side distension, or a lump-in-the-throat sensation - and clearly worsens with emotional upset, Liver Qi Stagnation is the likely root. The tongue often has a thin white coating, and the pulse feels wiry. This is the most common initial pattern, where constrained emotion disrupts the smooth flow of Qi.
When digestive complaints take centre stage - bloating, poor appetite, loose stools, and deep fatigue - the Spleen and Stomach Qi have been weakened. This often follows Liver Qi Stagnation, as the Liver overacts on the Spleen. The tongue appears pale and swollen with teeth marks, and the pulse is weak. This pattern explains the nagging gastrointestinal symptoms so many people experience.
If the Spleen deficiency persists, it generates dampness that congeals into phlegm, obstructing the channels. You may notice heavy limbs, persistent dull aches, and mental fogginess. The tongue coating becomes thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery. This Damp-Phlegm pattern often underlies the chronic, wandering pain that seems to have no clear cause.
In a smaller subset of people, long-standing stagnation turns into heat that disturbs the Heart. Heart Fire blazing brings palpitations, insomnia, a bitter taste in the mouth, and a red tongue tip with a rapid pulse. This pattern points to a more agitated, restless state that needs cooling and calming.
When the condition has worn on for years or there is a constitutional weakness, Kidney Yin Deficiency may appear. Chronic low-back soreness, night sweats, a dry mouth, and a red tongue with little coating are the hallmarks. The pulse is thin and rapid. This pattern is less common but signals deeper depletion.

patterns.symptoms: ["Wandering pain or distension in the chest and ribs", "Sensation of a lump in the throat (plum pit)", "Frequent sighing and irritability", "Symptoms worsen with emotional stress"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and frustration, Suppressing feelings, Heavy, greasy meals, Cold or raw foods, Sitting for long periods
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement (walking, yoga), Expressing emotions (crying, talking), Mint or chamomile tea, Warmth on the abdomen, Deep breathing and sighing
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress and frustration cause the Liver's Qi to become stuck, like a traffic jam in the body's flow. This stagnation creates pressure and distension in the chest and ribs, and the disrupted Qi can manifest as wandering aches, a lump sensation in the throat, and digestive upset. Because the Liver governs the smooth flow of emotions, the stuck Qi also amplifies irritability and anxiety, creating a vicious cycle that fuels the many unexplained physical symptoms of somatoform disorder.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Normal or slightly dark body, red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: Wiry (xian), like a taut guitar string, most prominent at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and emotional suppression directly cause Liver Qi to stagnate, so expressing feelings and reducing stress are essential. Gentle movement and warmth help to physically unblock Qi flow, while cold and greasy foods create internal dampness that further clogs the Liver’s ability to spread Qi. Sighing is a natural reflex to release stuck Qi, and aromatic herbs like mint mimic that action by dispersing Liver Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, regular meals with lightly cooked greens and aromatic herbs like mint and basil to gently move Qi. Avoid heavy, greasy, or cold foods that can further stagnate digestion. Incorporate daily gentle movement like walking, yoga, or tai chi to keep Qi flowing. Practice deep breathing or journaling to release emotional tension.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When the Spleen and Stomach Qi are weak, the body's ability to transform food into energy and blood is compromised. This leads to a general lack of nourishment that causes the fatigue, weak limbs, and mental fogginess often seen in somatoform disorder. The failure to transport fluids also creates dampness, which produces the persistent bloating, loose stools, and a heavy, sluggish feeling that shifts around the abdomen.
Because Qi is insufficient to support the mind, worry and overthinking become a habitual loop - the very mental state that further weakens the Spleen, locking the person in a cycle of digestive distress and vague, wandering body complaints that never seem to settle.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with scalloped edges and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and forceless, especially at the right Guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen's job is to transform food into Qi and transport fluids. It thrives on warmth and regular, gentle nourishment, and it is weakened by cold, dampness, and mental overwork. Raw and cold foods directly chill the digestive fire, while worry knots the Qi, making the Spleen unable to do its job. Warm meals, rest, and light movement support the Spleen's natural rhythm, allowing Qi and blood to be produced and distributed, which gradually lifts the fatigue and settles the vague body complaints.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like soups, congees, and stewed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat at regular times and stop just before feeling full. Gentle daily movement - a short walk after meals - helps Qi move without exhausting it. Protect the abdomen from cold and dampness.

patterns.better_with: Warm, dry environment, Light exercise like walking, Eating warm, cooked meals, Rest and calm
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weakened by worry, overthinking, or poor diet, it fails to transform fluids properly. Dampness builds up and congeals into Phlegm, a heavy, sticky substance that clogs the channels and collaterals. This obstruction produces the hallmark sensations of heaviness, numbness, and dull, persistent aches in the limbs and body. Phlegm also rises to cloud the mind, causing brain fog, muzzy-headedness, and dizziness, while its presence in the middle burner creates chest stuffiness, bloating, nausea, and a poor appetite.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with scalloped tooth marks, a wet surface, and a thick, white, greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (Hua) like a bead rolling through oil, or soggy (Ru) in the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm and Dampness are yin pathogens that thrive in cold, wet environments and are produced when the Spleen is sluggish. Cold and raw foods, overeating, and a sedentary lifestyle all weaken the Spleen and add more Dampness, thickening the Phlegm. Warmth, gentle movement, and light, cooked foods help the Spleen transform fluids, while a calm mind prevents the overthinking that directly injures Spleen Qi. This breaks the cycle of stagnation and heaviness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet foods, as well as dairy, which all create Dampness. Favor warm, cooked meals like soups, stews, and lightly steamed vegetables with gentle spices such as ginger. Eat at regular times and stop before feeling completely full. Gentle daily movement-walking, tai chi, or yoga-helps circulate Qi and transform Dampness. Keep your living space dry and airy, and avoid sitting in damp or cold environments for long periods.

patterns.better_with: Cool, quiet environment, Cold or room-temperature drinks, Cooling foods (cucumber, melon, mung bean), Deep breathing or meditation, Gentle exercise in the evening
patterns.why_this_happens:
When emotional stress and frustration linger unresolved, the Liver’s Qi flow stagnates and eventually generates heat. This heat can flare upward and harass the Heart, which houses the mind and spirit. The result is a restless, agitated state where the mind cannot settle - producing palpitations, insomnia, and a constant sense of inner heat.
Because the Heart opens into the tongue and governs blood circulation, the fire often shows up as mouth ulcers with red edges, a bitter taste, and a flushed face. The same internal fire can make ordinary bodily sensations feel exaggerated and distressing, which is why people with this pattern often experience burning pains or a feeling of heat in the chest even when no organic cause is found.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body with a distinctly redder tip, often with swollen red points at the tip; yellow dry coating. Pulse: Rapid and forceful, overflowing (Hong) especially at the left cun (front) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress, especially anger and frustration, stirs up Liver Qi which turns into heat and rushes to the Heart - exactly the mechanism behind this pattern. Spicy food, alcohol, and hot environments add external heat that intensifies the internal fire. Cooling foods and drinks counteract that heat, while rest and calming practices directly soothe the agitated Heart and help the mind settle, breaking the cycle of fire flaring upward.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and warming foods such as chili, lamb, and alcohol, as they add fuel to the fire. Instead, emphasize cooling, calming foods like cucumber, bitter melon, lotus root, and mung bean soup. Sip chrysanthemum or peppermint tea to gently clear heat. Wind down before bed with a screen-free routine, and try slow, diaphragmatic breathing to settle the mind. Even a short daily meditation or walk in nature can prevent heat from building up.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Kidney Yin is the body's deep reserve of cooling and moisture. When it runs low - from chronic stress, overwork, or constitutional weakness - the body loses its ability to lubricate the channels and calm the nervous system.
This gives rise to a deep, persistent soreness in the lower back and knees, along with a sensation of heat in the palms, soles, and chest. The empty heat rises to disturb the Heart, causing anxiety, palpitations, and insomnia, which are often experienced as part of the somatoform picture.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with little or no coating, dry surface, possible cracks. Pulse: fine and rapid (xi shu), weak at the left Chi position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is the body's cooling and moistening reserve. Overwork, late nights, and stress burn Yin, generating empty heat that worsens dry mouth, night sweats, and chronic pain. Rest, cooling foods, and adequate sleep replenish Yin and calm the deficiency fire, easing symptoms.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening foods like pears, black sesame, and congee. Avoid spicy, drying foods and excessive sweating. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, which further depletes Yin.

faqs.question: Is my pain real if doctors can't find a cause?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, your pain is a genuine signal of disharmony in the body's Qi, Blood, or organ systems. Even if imaging and lab tests are normal, the sensations you feel reflect a functional imbalance that is just as real as a structural one. TCM does not dismiss these symptoms - it takes them as the starting point for diagnosis.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help with symptoms that have no physical explanation?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture works by unblocking the flow of Qi along specific channels. When Qi stagnates or becomes deficient, it can create pain, pressure, or other sensations even without tissue damage. By inserting fine needles at precise points, acupuncture restores smooth flow and rebalances the organ systems involved. Many patients feel immediate relief of muscle tension or a sense of calm after a session, and cumulative treatments address the deeper pattern.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my antidepressant medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases TCM can safely complement conventional medications. However, some herbs may interact with SSRIs or SNRIs, so it is essential to inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about everything you are taking. Never stop or adjust your medication without medical supervision. Acupuncture is generally safe to combine with medication and may even help reduce side effects like fatigue or nausea.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: No. Herbal formulas are typically used for a defined period - usually several weeks to a few months - to correct the underlying imbalance. Once the pattern resolves and symptoms stabilize, the formula is adjusted, reduced, or stopped. Some people with chronic, deep-rooted deficiency may benefit from occasional maintenance formulas, but the goal is always independence, not lifelong reliance.

faqs.question: What if my symptoms change over time?
faqs.answer: It's very common for symptoms to shift as treatment progresses, and this is actually a good sign - it means the body is responding. A skilled TCM practitioner will adjust your herbal formula and acupuncture points at each visit to follow the changing pattern. This dynamic, personalized approach is one of TCM's strengths for conditions like somatoform disorder.

faqs.question: How soon will I notice a difference?
faqs.answer: Many people feel a sense of calm or reduced pain after the very first acupuncture session. Herbal formulas often take a few days to a week to show their effect. Significant, lasting change usually builds over 6-12 weeks of consistent treatment. The timeline depends on your specific pattern and how long the imbalance has been present.

research.title: Acupuncture for patients with somatoform disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This systematic review included 15 RCTs with over 1,200 participants and found that acupuncture, either alone or combined with conventional medication, significantly reduced somatic symptom severity scores compared to sham acupuncture or medication alone. The effect was most pronounced for pain and gastrointestinal symptoms, and the treatment was well-tolerated with minimal side effects.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Acupuncture for patients with somatoform disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Psychosomatic Research. 2020; 134: 110128.

research.title: Xiao Yao San for somatoform disorder with Liver Qi Stagnation: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this 8-week RCT of 96 patients, those receiving modified Xiao Yao San showed a significantly greater reduction in Somatic Symptom Scale scores and Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores compared to the placebo group. The formula was particularly effective for chest tightness, globus sensation, and irritability.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Modified Xiao Yao San for somatoform disorder with Liver Qi Stagnation: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2019; 25(8): 607-613.

research.title: Electroacupuncture versus paroxetine for somatoform disorder: a comparative effectiveness study
research.description: This trial compared electroacupuncture at Baihui DU-20, Neiguan PC-6, and Taichong LR-3 with paroxetine in 80 patients. Both groups improved, but the acupuncture group had a faster onset of symptom relief and fewer side effects, with benefits maintained at 3-month follow-up.
research.periodical: Wang H, et al. Electroacupuncture versus paroxetine for somatoform disorder: a randomized controlled trial. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2018; 2018: 6287504.
